title: Life Admin · Episode 1
chapters: Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax
Cutting your power and water bills

units.t: Life Admin. Episode one.
In this episode: Reading your payslip, Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax and Cutting your power and water bills.
Part one. Reading your payslip.
That little document on payday tells you whether you are being paid correctly.
Most people never really read it.
Here is how.
Why your payslip matters.
Imagine working the same Saturday shifts for a year, only to discover your weekend penalty rate was never applied.
Underpayment is more common than many people realise, and it is not always deliberate.
Payroll errors, wrong award classifications and outdated rates all happen, and your payslip is where they show up first.
In Australia, employers generally must give employees a payslip within one working day of payday, on paper or electronically.
Reading it takes two minutes each pay and can save you hundreds or thousands of dollars.
This is general information, not legal or financial advice.
The Fair Work Ombudsman, fairwork.
gov.
au, is the official place to check your situation.
What must be on it.
A compliant payslip names your employer, including their ABN, and names you.
It shows the pay period and the date you were paid.
Gross pay is your total before tax.
Net pay is what lands in your bank account.
It should also list deductions such as tax or salary sacrifice, plus any bonuses, loadings, allowances or penalty rates.
If you are paid by the hour, it shows your hourly rate and the hours paid at that rate.
It shows the superannuation your employer is paying and the fund it is going to.
If any of this is missing, politely ask your payroll team why.
Tax and super.
Under the pay as you go system, your employer withholds tax and sends it to the Australian Taxation Office.
The amount depends on your earnings, how often you are paid and your tax file number declaration.
Claim the tax-free threshold from one employer only; claiming it in two jobs can leave you with a bill at tax time.
Super is paid on top of your wages.
The super guarantee is a percentage of your ordinary time earnings, 12 per cent since 1 July 2025; the ATO website lists the current rate.
Since 1 July 2026, employers must pay super each payday, and it should reach your fund within seven business days.
A payslip only shows what your employer says it paid, so check your fund's app or myGov regularly.
Rates, penalties and awards.
Many Australian workers are covered by a modern award, a legal document that sets minimum pay and conditions for an industry or occupation.
Others are covered by an enterprise agreement negotiated at their workplace.
These set your minimum base rate and extras such as casual loading, overtime and penalty rates for evenings, weekends and public holidays.
To check yours, use the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator or download your award's pay guide.
You will need your award, your classification level and whether you are full time, part time or casual.
Minimum rates are usually reviewed each year, with changes commonly starting from the first full pay period on or after 1 July.
A rate that was right last year might be wrong now.
Routine and fixing errors.
Keep a note of your hours each week, including start and finish times and breaks.
When your payslip arrives, compare the hours with your record and check that each type, such as overtime or Sunday work, has the right rate.
Glance at the year to date totals and your leave balance.
Save every payslip as a PDF in one folder, because records are your best evidence.
If something looks wrong, write to your manager or payroll.
Say what you noticed, what you believe is correct and how you worked it out, and keep a copy.
If it is not fixed, the Fair Work Ombudsman offers free help, and the ATO handles unpaid super.
Time limits apply to recovering wages, so act early.
Employers must not punish you for raising a genuine concern.
The key idea: Your payslip is your best everyday check that you are being paid what you are owed.
Part two. Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax.
Staying with the same provider for years can quietly cost you.
A little comparison, a phone call and a calendar reminder can trim your household bills without changing how you live.
The loyalty tax.
Picture two neighbours with identical houses and habits.
One signed up with an energy retailer a decade ago and never looked again.
The other compares plans each year.
The first often pays noticeably more, because a discount expired or cheaper plans arrived that they never moved to.
This pattern, sometimes called the loyalty tax, shows up across energy, phone, internet and insurance.
Providers rely on inertia.
The fix is not constant switching.
Choose one month, perhaps around tax time, and review every regular bill in a single sitting.
Start with your latest bills: usage, daily supply charge, rates, any time-of-use pricing and your solar feed-in tariff.
Compare energy officially.
For electricity and gas, use free government comparison sites rather than commercial ones that may be paid by retailers.
In New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and the ACT, the Australian Energy Regulator runs Energy Made Easy at energymadeeasy.
gov.
au.
In Victoria, use Victorian Energy Compare.
Western Australia and the Northern Territory have different market arrangements, with fewer choices in many areas.
Enter your usage or upload a bill to see plans at your address.
In many states retailers must show how offers compare with a government reference price.
Look past headline discounts: conditional discounts that vanish if you pay late can make a plan dearer than it looks.
Switching and right-sizing.
Changing energy retailers usually involves no physical work.
The same poles, wires and meter supply you, and only the company billing you changes.
The new retailer arranges the transfer.
Check for exit fees and contract end dates.
You can usually keep your mobile number, and month-to-month plans leave you free to go.
Sometimes just telling your provider you are thinking of leaving gets you a better plan.
Many people pay for more mobile data or home internet speed than they use.
Check your usage in your provider's app, then choose a plan with a modest buffer.
On the NBN, typical evening speeds matter more than maximums.
Cancel streaming services and subscriptions you no longer use.
Hardship help.
If paying bills is becoming hard, act before disconnection notices arrive.
Energy retailers must have hardship programs, which can include payment plans, advice on cutting usage and protection from disconnection while you take part.
Telcos have financial hardship policies too.
Ask for the hardship team by name.
State and territory governments offer energy concessions and rebates to eligible people, such as pensioners, healthcare card holders and some low-income households.
These are not always applied automatically, so check your state government's website.
Services Australia can tell you which cards and payments you may qualify for.
The free National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007, connects you with a financial counsellor who can negotiate with providers for you.
When things go wrong.
Billing errors, surprise fees and botched transfers do happen.
Contact the provider, explain the problem clearly and ask for a complaint reference number.
Keep notes of every call, including the date and the name of the person you spoke with.
If the problem isn't fixed, you can go to an independent ombudsman for free.
For phone and internet, that is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman.
For energy and water, most states have their own energy and water ombudsman scheme, so check which applies in your state.
Ombudsmen can investigate and, in many cases, require providers to fix the problem or pay compensation.
This is general information; check moneysmart.
gov.
au and your state's consumer affairs website.
The key idea: Long-term customers often pay more than new ones, so check your deals once a year.
Part three. Cutting your power and water bills.
Your energy bill is a story about heat: heating rooms, heating water and keeping food cold.
Read it properly and you can find real savings without living in the dark.
Read your bill.
Look past the total on your electricity bill.
The daily supply charge is a fixed amount you pay just to be connected.
The usage charge is a price per kilowatt hour, kWh, the unit your meter counts.
One kWh is a 1,000 watt appliance running for an hour.
Time of use plans charge more at peak times.
Watch your average daily use as you make changes.
People often start by unplugging phone chargers, which is like skipping a mint while buying a new car.
In most Australian homes, heating and cooling are the biggest users, then water heating, then fridges, dryers and pool pumps.
To find big users, multiply wattage by hours.
A 2,400 watt heater running five hours a night uses 12 kilowatt hours.
Heating and cooling smarter.
A reverse cycle air conditioner is a heat pump.
Rather than turning electricity directly into heat, it moves heat from outside to inside.
It can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity, which typically makes it far cheaper to run than a plug-in bar or fan heater.
Thermostat settings matter too.
Australian energy agencies commonly suggest around 18 to 20 degrees in winter and 25 to 27 in summer, and each extra degree adds noticeably to running costs.
Heat or cool only the rooms you use.
Seal draughts around doors and windows with weather strips and door snakes.
Close curtains on winter nights, and block summer sun with external shading, which works better than internal blinds.
Hot water, fridge, standby.
Every hot shower costs you twice: once for the water and again to heat it.
A showerhead with a good Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards, WELS, star rating uses less hot water, and cutting a shower by a couple of minutes adds up over a year.
Fix dripping hot taps quickly and wash clothes in cold water.
Your fridge runs all day, so keep it at around 3 to 4 degrees and the freezer around minus 18.
Check the door seals by closing the door on a sheet of paper to see if it holds, and leave space behind for air.
An old second fridge in the garage can be surprisingly expensive to run.
Walk through your home at night and count the glowing standby lights.
Switch off consoles and spare devices at the wall.
Saving water.
A toilet with a slow leak into the bowl can waste a large amount of water without anyone noticing.
Test yours by adding a few drops of food colouring to the cistern and waiting about 15 minutes without flushing.
If colour appears in the bowl, the cistern is leaking and needs repair.
Most plumbing repairs need a licensed plumber.
Use the half flush button where you have one.
Run dishwashers and washing machines only when full, and look for good WELS star ratings when buying them.
Outside, water the garden early in the morning or in the evening so less is lost to evaporation, and use mulch to keep soil moist.
Check local water restrictions and rebates.
Buy smart, shop around.
The Energy Rating Label shows a star rating and an estimated yearly energy use in kWh, the best number for comparing models of a similar size.
A cheaper appliance with a poor rating can cost more over its life than a pricier efficient one.
Many households stay on the same plan for years and pay more than they need to.
Compare plans every year or so.
The government's Energy Made Easy website, energymadeeasy.
gov.
au, compares offers in most states and territories, and Victoria has its own Victorian Energy Compare site.
Ask your retailer if they have a better plan.
If you hold a pension, health care or other concession card, ask about energy concessions.
If you are struggling to pay, contact your retailer early about hardship programs.
This is general information only.
The key idea: Bills combine a daily supply charge with a price per kilowatt hour, and heating, cooling and hot water are the big users.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is it worth reading your payslip every pay?
Answer. It is where pay errors, such as a missing penalty rate, show up first.
Question two. What does the 'loyalty tax' refer to?
Answer. Loyal customers often paying more than new ones.
Question three. Which usually uses the most energy in an Australian home?
Answer. Heating and cooling.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
